alt: Rights and justice at the centre linked to the four core concepts: power (who defines or enforces a right), sovereignty (a state’s claim to decide rights internally against universal claims), legitimacy (whether a claim or its denial is accepted) and interdependence (pressure and obligations beyond the state).
caption: The same four concepts structure every rights answer.

after: ## Worked example: applying the four concepts to a rights issue
alt: Four questions to work through in order: who has the power to define or enforce the right; whether the state claims sovereign authority and how that meets international frameworks; whether positions are accepted as legitimate; and what pressures or obligations reach actors beyond the state.
caption: Work through all four concepts explicitly rather than describing the issue.

alt: Anchors for a rights case log: the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights; international bodies (ICJ, UN Human Rights Council, UNHCR, ICC); regional courts in Europe, the Americas and Africa; the Responsibility to Protect norm; and civil society organisations such as Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International.
caption: Precise names of frameworks and institutions are part of what Paper 2 rewards.

after: ## Comparing across the three thematic studies
alt: A triangle of the three thematic studies. Rights and justice links to peace and conflict, where conflict raises rights violations for the same population, and to development and sustainability, where unequal outcomes raise questions of distributive justice. The same four core concepts apply throughout.
caption: Real issues cross theme boundaries; so should your examples.

alt: Paper 2 has two sections. In section A candidates answer one thematic-study-specific essay, one set per thematic study. In section B they answer one integrating essay linking all three thematic studies and the core topics.
caption: One thematic essay plus one integrating essay: practise both with rights content.
